title: The Concrete Problem: Student Placement & Feature Space
script: Welcome to NeuraMind. To understand the Perceptron with genuine mathematical depth, we begin not with abstractions, but with a real classification challenge: predicting college student placement. Consider a dataset with two continuous input features: a student's I Q, denoted as x 1, and their college C G P A, denoted as x 2. The target label y is binary: one represents Placed, while zero represents Not Placed. When we plot these students into a two dimensional coordinate space with I Q on the horizontal axis and C G P A on the vertical axis, the data naturally forms two clusters. The fundamental objective of the perceptron is to automatically discover a dividing boundary that cleanly isolates placed students from unplaced students.
subtitle: Task: Predict Placement (y in {0,1}) from IQ (x1) and CGPA (x2) in 2D Feature Space

title: Artificial Neuron Architecture & Matrix Dot Product Flow
script: How does the artificial neuron process this information? Let us examine the linear algebra and matrix data flow. Each student is represented as an input feature vector x with dimension D. We introduce a weight vector w of matching dimension, and a scalar bias b. In compact matrix notation, we augment the input vector by prepending a constant one at index zero. This combines the bias directly into our augmented weight vector. The forward pass computes the vector dot product: z equals w transpose times x plus b, which is the sum of each feature multiplied by its corresponding weight. Consider a test applicant with I Q of 100 and C G P A of 5.1. With candidate weights of 1.0 for I Q, 2.0 for C G P A, and a bias of minus 105.0, the dot product z evaluates to positive 5.2. Passing this value through the Heaviside step activation function, since 5.2 is greater than zero, the output evaluates to one, predicting placement. Notice also feature importance: because the weight for C G P A is double that of I Q, changes in C G P A have twice the mathematical impact on the final decision.
subtitle: Augmented Matrix Flow: z = w~^T x~ = b + w1*x1 + w2*x2 -> Step(z) -> y_hat

title: Geometric Decision Boundary & Slope-Intercept Form
script: Now let us examine the geometry of this calculation. The decision boundary occurs exactly where the dot product z equals zero. In our two dimensional feature space, this equation is w 1 x 1 plus w 2 x 2 plus b equals zero. By rearranging this algebraic expression into standard slope intercept form, x 2 equals minus w 1 over w 2 times x 1, minus b over w 2. This reveals the precise physical meaning of our model parameters. The slope m is governed entirely by the ratio of the weights, determining the orientation and angle of the decision boundary. The vertical intercept c is governed by the bias b, which shifts the line parallel across the coordinate plane without altering its angle. Furthermore, the weight vector w acts as the normal vector perpendicular to the line, pointing directly into the positive half space where predictions evaluate to one, while the opposing half space represents class zero.
subtitle: Boundary: w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b = 0 => x2 = -(w1/w2)*x1 - (b/w2) | Normal w points to z >= 0

title: Learning Mechanics, Error Discrepancy & Vector Updates
script: How does an untrained perceptron discover optimal weights? Through the Perceptron Learning Rule. Suppose an untrained line misclassifies a placed student with label one as unplaced with prediction zero. The error term, y minus y hat, evaluates to plus one. To correct this, we update parameters by adding the learning rate eta multiplied by the input coordinates. This vector addition rotates and pulls the decision boundary directly toward the misclassified sample. Conversely, if an unplaced student is misclassified into the positive region, the error term evaluates to minus one, subtracting the vector and pushing the boundary away. When predictions are correct, the error is zero and parameters remain unchanged. Mathematically, this unified update rule corresponds to executing stochastic gradient descent on the Perceptron Loss function, which penalizes samples proportional to their distance across the wrong side of the margin.
subtitle: Unified Rule: w_new = w_old + eta*(y - y_hat)*x | SGD on Loss L = max(0, -y*f(x))

title: Real-Time Training Simulation & Parameter Evolution
script: Let us observe this training process in action across real student data. We initialize the perceptron with arbitrary random weights. Initially, the boundary cuts through the dataset, producing multiple misclassifications highlighted by pulsing red indicators. In the first iteration, an error triggers an update, adjusting the weight vector and shifting the decision line. In the second iteration, another misclassified point pulls the boundary further into alignment, reducing errors to one. Finally, the remaining error is resolved. The boundary settles cleanly between the two classes, achieving zero misclassifications and complete linear convergence.
subtitle: Simulation: Live parameter updates resolve errors 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 0 (Convergence)

title: Line-by-Line Python NumPy Implementation
script: Now let us examine how this theory translates into production Python code using NumPy. In the init method, we define the learning rate and training epochs. In the fit method, we first call n p dot insert to prepend a column of ones to our feature matrix, augmenting it for the bias term. We initialize our parameter vector w to zeros. In the training loop, for each training instance, we compute the scalar dot product z, apply the Heaviside step threshold to produce y hat, and execute the unified weight update rule whenever an error occurs. Finally, the predict method processes entire batches of unseen test students simultaneously using vectorized matrix multiplication.
subtitle: Code: np.insert(bias) -> dot product z -> Step threshold -> Unified update -> Batch predict

title: Convergence Graph, Generalization & The XOR Failure
script: Examining the training curve on the right, we observe the classification error plunge rapidly to zero as the model converges. On the left, the shaded decision regions demonstrate model generalization, proving that any new student applicant is accurately mapped to their appropriate class. However, we must confront the fundamental limitation of a single perceptron: it can only solve linearly separable problems. When presented with non linear distributions such as the X O R problem, where positive instances lie diagonally opposite, a single straight line can never succeed. To overcome this barrier, deep learning stacks multiple artificial neurons into hidden layers, forming Multi-Layer Perceptrons capable of bending decision surfaces to approximate any complex mathematical function.
subtitle: Convergence to 0 Loss | Generalization Mesh | Stacking Perceptrons Solves Non-Linear XOR
